name: Slime
origin: Dragon Quest (Square Enix / Enix; art by Akira Toriyama)
facts: Slimes debuted in the 1986 game Dragon Quest as the first and weakest enemy, and have appeared in almost every game since.
Yuji Horii said the idea came from slime-like characters in Wizardry. He conceived a pile of goo; Akira Toriyama's design came back as a teardrop the team considered perfect.
They became the series mascot: often easy to defeat, sometimes friendly townspeople who say they are not a bad slime, with a 'slurp' verbal tic. Spin-offs even star a nation of slimes.
The same article lists many varieties, including differently colored slimes, She-Slimes, Bubble Slimes, Healslimes, and crowned King Slimes, plus a rare Metal Slime family.

name: Metal slime
facts: The metal slime debuts in the first Dragon Quest. It looks like an ordinary slime except for a silver-grey metallic body.

It is infamous for a very high experience payout, rare appearances, and a habit of running away. High agility and defence mean ordinary attacks usually miss or barely hurt it, and most spells do nothing.
Horii explained the fleeing as shyness. Fans treat meeting one as a jackpot rather than a threat, because it looks almost identical to a normal slime.

name: King slime
facts: A king slime is a giant crown-wearing blob made when multiple ordinary slimes fuse. It wears a gold-rimmed crown, and an optional Dragon Quest VIII scene shows the crown is what holds the fusion together: remove it and the king splits.

Players often meet a group of slimes that call more of their kind; when eight gather, they pile up into one king slime. The monster is a large step up from a normal slime and often knows supportive magic.
The game debut was Dragon Quest IV, after an earlier manga appearance. The crowned fusion is a recurring series monster, not a one-off boss.

name: Dragonlord
facts: The Dragonlord is the final boss of the original Dragon Quest. He steals the Sphere of Light from Tantegel, covers Alefgard in darkness, and kidnaps Princess Gwaelin.
He first appears as a blue-skinned humanoid in a purple robe with a dragon-carved staff, then reveals an upright bipedal dragon form.

Cornered, he offers the hero half the world. In the 1986 release, accepting ends the game as a failure. The offer itself was unusual for a villain of that year: a political deal, not mindless rampage.

name: Cactuar
origin: Final Fantasy (Square Enix; Japanese name Sabotender)
facts: Cactuars are anthropomorphic cacti with haniwa-like faces, usually drawn in a running pose. They first appear as enemies in Final Fantasy VI and became a series mascot beside the chocobo and the moogle. The franchise is owned by Square Enix.

Tetsuya Nomura based the face on a high-school doodle. They are notoriously hard to hit. Their famous attack is 1000 Needles, a defensive strike that deals a fixed 1000 hit points regardless of defence. In Final Fantasy XV, common cactuars are rare spawns that try to run, and beating them pays well in experience.

name: Behemoth (Final Fantasy)
origin: Final Fantasy, using a biblical name
facts: Final Fantasy behemoths are large, often late-game beasts. They first appear as a boss in Final Fantasy II. Many depictions are large purple beasts that gore with horns and lightning, on four legs or two, and answer a spell with a bigger spell such as Flare or Meteor. A stronger King Behemoth also recurs.

The name is the beast from Job 40. The biblical Behemoth is a primeval land monster paired with Leviathan, so powerful that the text says only God can overcome it. The Hebrew word is an augmentative of 'beast'.

name: Final Fantasy summon (Esper / Aeon pattern)
facts: Summoning, proposed for the first game and first shipped in Final Fantasy III, calls a monster to perform a cinematic action. Summons may be optional or tied to the story.

Their names are drawn from many cultures, including Egyptian, Middle Eastern, Asian, and Classical myth. Group labels across the series include Espers, Guardian Forces, Aeons, Eidolons, Astrals, Primals, and Eikons.
Final Fantasy VI's Espers are that game's summons. Ifrit, Shiva, Bahamut, and Odin are named as recurring examples. Dead espers leave magicite that teaches spells.
Separately, Arabic cosmography describes Bahamut as a giant fish that helps hold up the world, a name later linked to the biblical Behemoth. That fish is not what the FFVI sentence describes.

EarthBound itself parodies RPG habits in a modern, deliberately goofy setting: pencil erasers, hallucinations, and battles with piles of vomit.

facts: Breath of Fire's backstory says the goddess Myria offered to grant any wish and split the Dragon Clan into Light and Dark dragons. She was sealed by the Light Dragons with six magic keys.
Emperor Zog's Dark Dragon empire wants to revive her and take the world. The hero Ryu is one of the last of a people who can turn into dragons.

name: Zakum
facts: Zakum is a spirit that was sealed in a tree in the El Nath mines. Miners' greed corrupted it. It forced the town to build a statue, possessed the statue, and killed the town. The forest withered and the dead walked.

The fight is summoned with an Eye of Fire on an altar. Players can destroy its arms to take away arm slams and claps; late in the fight the arms go away and the cracked body remains. Easy, Normal, and Chaos versions exist.

name: Horntail
facts: Horntail is an evil three-headed dragon, one of the Great Kings of Minar Forest. He rebelled against the dragon chief Nine Spirit, stole Nine Spirit's egg, broke a pact with the Halflingers, and hid in a cave to heal while plotting a wider rule.
The chronicle says the three heads mean three minds. The battle is phased. Easy, Normal, and Chaos entries exist, and for a time Horntail was treated as the game's top boss after Zakum.

name: Pink Bean
facts: Pink Bean is a strange creature from another world, a major boss in the Temple of Time. Kirston tried to use the Mirror of the Goddess to summon the Black Mage and got Pink Bean instead. The chronicle says it is cute, absurdly powerful, and able to revive a dead god.

The fight starts with five god-statues, while Pink Bean lounges, summons mini beans, and later steps off a throne. On defeat it cries and hops through a portal. A non-canon note places it in Bean World opposite Black Bean. Trivia says it eats meat, plays guitar, and wears headphones.
The wiki's Taiwan server row says the boss was formerly named 皮卡啾, glossed on that page as Pikachu, and is now 粉豆 (Pink Bean). That former label is an IP collision to avoid, not a design to reuse.

name: Papulatus
facts: Papulatus came through the Dimensional Crack. The chronicle says it has many personalities, all of them evil, warped Ludibrium's toys into monsters, and grows stronger as the crack widens.

The wiki places the boss at the bottom of Ludibrium's clocktower and says it is a ghostly plant-like being from another dimension who pilots a robot shaped like a clock. An alarm phase rains clock springs. When the first phase ends, the clock robot explodes and Papulatus fights from a smaller vehicle.
It is summoned with a Piece of Cracked Dimension. The Japanese server name on the page is Vicious Plant.

name: First partner Pokémon (elemental trio)
origin: Pokémon (Game Freak / Nintendo / The Pokémon Company). Archetype only; no species is proposed for copying.
facts: Bulbapedia, citing official usage, describes a first partner Pokémon (long called a starter) as the first creature a trainer owns. In the core games a professor usually offers a Grass-, Fire-, or Water-type.

Those three types are a rock-paper-scissors lesson: Fire beats Grass, Water beats Fire, Grass beats Water. The first partner is used to battle the first wild creature, and is often kept as the partner the trainer trusts most. They are said to be extremely rare in the wild.

Pokémon as a franchise is creatures with special powers living alongside humans. Battles are non-lethal: a defeated Pokémon faints. Trainers catch species with Poké Balls and log them in a Pokédex. The name Pokémon and the species names are owned through The Pokémon Company (Nintendo, Creatures, and Game Freak).

name: Legendary Pokémon
facts: Bulbapedia describes Legendary Pokémon as incredibly rare and often very powerful, written into the world's myths, sometimes worshipped as deities. There is no single mechanical test; official media is what places a creature in the group.
A related but separate group, Mythical Pokémon, is usually event-exclusive. Western material folded mythicals into legendaries before Generation V.
Wikipedia records the April 1996 'Legendary Pokémon Offer' in CoroCoro, built around Mew, a secret creature added late, not obtainable by normal play, and meant for a promotion.

name: Powerhouse Pokémon (fan term: pseudo-legendary)
facts: Bulbapedia's Powerhouse Pokémon, which fans call pseudo-legendaries, are the final stage of a three-stage line, with a base stat total of exactly 600 before any mega form, and a slow experience curve (1,250,000 points to level 100).

They are usually harder to raise than ordinary creatures and often Dragon-type. Every generation has added at least one, typically late in that generation's dex, just before the legendaries. 'Powerhouse Pokémon' has been used in official merchandise and news; 'pseudo-legendary' remains a fan term.
